articles.title: A Diet Built to Lower Blood Pressure Just Beat Five Rivals at Protecting the Aging Brain
articles.excerpt: In a Harvard-led comparison of nearly 160,000 people, the DASH eating pattern outperformed the Mediterranean diet and four others, with the most faithful followers showing a 41 percent lower risk of cognitive decline decades later.
articles.image_caption: A Harvard-led study found the DASH eating pattern was the strongest dietary predictor of late-life cognitive health
articles.nri_angle: South Asians face an unusually high burden of both hypertension and dementia, yet the brain-protective DASH pattern — heavy on vegetables, fruit, whole grains, beans and low-fat dairy, light on salt and sweets — maps neatly onto a thoughtfully built Indian thali, giving NRI families a culturally familiar template that may guard the heart and the mind at once.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: People Born With Naturally Lower Cholesterol Are Far Less Likely to Develop Dementia, a Million-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Using genetics to sidestep the bias of ordinary diet studies, researchers found that a modest lifelong reduction in cholesterol — the same effect statins aim for — was linked to a sharply lower risk of dementia, hinting that protecting the heart may also protect the mind.
articles.image_caption: A study of more than a million people linked genetically lower cholesterol to a sharply reduced risk of dementia
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry both elevated heart-disease risk and a high genetic predisposition to unhealthy cholesterol, and statins are already among the most prescribed drugs in Indian households — so evidence that lifelong lower cholesterol may also guard against dementia gives the diaspora one more reason to take a number they were already told to watch seriously.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Diet and Exercise Beat a Popular Diabetes Pill at Holding Off Multiple Diseases, a 21-Year Trial Finds
articles.excerpt: Following adults with prediabetes for more than two decades, researchers found that an intensive diet-and-exercise program — not the widely prescribed drug metformin — was tied to a meaningfully lower risk of piling up multiple chronic illnesses, with the sharpest protection against the costliest disease combinations.
articles.image_caption: A 21-year trial found an intensive diet-and-exercise program lowered the long-term risk of multiple chronic diseases (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: Metformin is one of the most commonly prescribed drugs across Indian households at home and abroad, and many NRIs reach for the pill while treating diet and exercise as optional — so a 21-year trial showing that the lifestyle program, not the drug, blunted the long-term accumulation of chronic disease reframes what genuine prevention looks like for a diaspora at high metabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Out Sugar Entirely May Backfire on the Gut, a New Study Suggests — the Lesson Is Moderation, Not Zero
articles.excerpt: Mice fed a low-fat diet with no sugar at all developed a disrupted gut microbiome, worse blood-sugar control and signs of fatty liver — even though they did not gain weight — hinting that total elimination, rather than simply trimming excess, can undo the very benefits people are chasing.
articles.image_caption: A new study suggests removing sugar entirely from a low-fat diet may disrupt the gut microbiome (Wikimedia Commons)
articles.nri_angle: "Sugar-free" and "no sugar" have become aspirational badges in diaspora kitchens and on diabetes-conscious Indian menus, where cutting out mithai and refined carbs is treated as an unalloyed good — so a study warning that total elimination may disrupt gut and metabolic health adds a needed note of nuance for a community both highly sugar-aware and highly diabetes-prone.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Hours of Lifting a Week May Be a Sweet Spot for Living Longer, a 147,000-Person Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking more than 147,000 American adults for up to three decades, researchers found that 90 to 120 minutes of strength training each week was tied to a 13 percent lower risk of dying from any cause — with sharper drops for heart and neurological disease, and, tellingly, no extra payoff for grinding out more than two hours.
articles.image_caption: A new study links 90 to 120 minutes of weekly strength training to a lower risk of death from all causes
articles.nri_angle: Indians abroad carry an outsized burden of diabetes and heart disease, and the gyms many already pay for go underused — so a study pinpointing two hours of weekly lifting as a longevity sweet spot offers the diaspora a concrete, time-boxed target rather than a vague call to 'exercise more.'
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: How Old Do You Feel? Your Answer May Reveal How Well You're Sleeping, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: In more than 3,100 adults, those who felt older than their actual age reported markedly worse sleep — more insomnia, less regular sleep and greater daytime fatigue — and, through that poor sleep, worse physical health, suggesting a single honest question can flag a problem long before a clinic visit does.
articles.image_caption: Adults who felt older than their actual age reported more insomnia and poorer sleep, a new study found
articles.nri_angle: Chronically short, late and irregular nights are almost a way of life in the diaspora — split between work hours here and family calls to India — so a study showing that simply feeling older than your years is an early warning sign of poor sleep gives NRIs a quick, free self-check before fatigue hardens into ill health.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fish-Oil Pills Did Reach the Brain — but Did Nothing for Memory, a Two-Year Trial of At-Risk Adults Finds
articles.excerpt: In a rigorous double-blind study, high doses of the omega-3 DHA clearly raised omega-3 levels in the brains of older adults at risk for Alzheimer's, yet brought no improvement in memory, thinking or the shrinkage of the brain's memory centre — a sobering result for a supplement Americans spend over a billion dollars a year on.
articles.image_caption: A two-year trial found high-dose omega-3 DHA reached the brain but did not improve memory in adults at risk for Alzheimer's
articles.nri_angle: Fish-oil capsules are a fixture of the diaspora medicine cabinet — reached for as cheap insurance for the brain, especially in largely vegetarian Indian households that eat little oily fish — so a gold-standard trial showing the pills do not protect memory is a pointed reminder for NRI families to spend on the lifestyle basics that do, rather than on a supplement that does not.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Daily Multivitamin Modestly Slowed the Body's Biological Clock in a Two-Year Trial — but the Effect Was Small
articles.excerpt: Using 'epigenetic clocks' that read the chemical wear on DNA, researchers found older adults who took a daily multivitamin with cocoa flavanols for two years aged slightly more slowly at the cellular level than those on a placebo — a tantalising but modest result that sits alongside stronger evidence for diet and fitness.
articles.image_caption: A two-year trial linked a daily multivitamin with cocoa flavanols to a modest slowing of biological ageing on epigenetic clocks
articles.nri_angle: Multivitamins are a staple of NRI households — mailed to students abroad and pressed on ageing parents — so evidence that the pills nudge biological ageing only modestly, while diet and fitness move it far more, helps the diaspora spend its health budget where the returns are largest rather than on a daily tablet alone.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Fasting May Protect the Mind by Reshaping the Gut, a New Study on Stress and Depression Suggests
articles.excerpt: When stressed mice were put on a time-restricted eating schedule, they resisted depression-like behaviour, kept healthier insulation around their brain cells, and grew a more diverse gut microbiome — pointing to the gut-brain axis as a route to mental resilience.
articles.image_caption: A new study links time-restricted eating to a more diverse gut microbiome and greater resilience against stress-induced depression in mice.
articles.nri_angle: Many Indian families already practise periodic fasting for religious reasons — Ekadashi, Navratri, Karva Chauth, Ramadan — so research linking time-restricted eating to a healthier gut and steadier mood gives the diaspora a fresh, science-backed lens on a habit their traditions have long encouraged, at a time when immigrant stress and mental-health stigma run high.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Lose the Hidden Belly Fat and the Body Seems to Remember — Even After the Weight Comes Back, a 10-Year Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Following dieters for a decade with high-resolution MRI scans, researchers found that cutting visceral fat — the deep fat around the organs — left a lasting shield against type 2 diabetes, even in people who regained nearly all the weight they had lost.
articles.image_caption: A decade-long study used high-resolution MRI to track visceral fat, the deep fat around the organs that drives diabetes risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asians are famously prone to storing fat deep in the abdomen around their organs at low body weights — the 'thin-fat' build behind their outsized diabetes risk — so a study showing that shrinking visceral fat buys lasting protection, even after the scale creeps back, reframes what success means for diaspora families battling weight regain.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Order You Eat Your Food May Matter Almost as Much as What's On the Plate, a Glucose-Monitor Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Tracking real meals with continuous glucose monitors, researchers found that eating fibre and protein before the carbohydrates flattened the post-meal blood-sugar spike — in healthy people and those with type 2 diabetes alike.
articles.image_caption: Eating fibre and protein such as dal, vegetables and salad before the rice and roti blunted post-meal blood-sugar spikes in a glucose-monitor study
articles.nri_angle: The Indian plate is built around rice and roti, and South Asians carry an outsized, earlier-onset risk of type 2 diabetes — so a free, no-deprivation tweak like eating the dal, sabzi and salad before the rice offers diaspora families a way to keep their food and still blunt the blood-sugar spikes that drive that risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Weakening Muscles May Quietly Make It Easier for Cancer to Grow, New Research Suggests — and Exercise May Reverse It
articles.excerpt: A Duke-NUS study finds that as muscles lose strength with age, they stop sending out a protective molecular signal that helps hold tumours in check — and that exercise can switch that signal back on.
articles.image_caption: A Duke-NUS study suggests maintaining muscle through resistance exercise may help keep the body's anti-cancer signalling active with age
articles.nri_angle: South Asians tend to carry less muscle and more fat at any given weight — the so-called 'thin-fat' body type — which leaves many in the diaspora vulnerable to age-related muscle loss even when the scale looks fine, making the study's message that strength training protects against more than just frailty especially relevant.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Exercise May Work as Well as Pills or Therapy for Depression and Anxiety, a Review of Hundreds of Trials Finds
articles.excerpt: An umbrella analysis of hundreds of clinical studies involving tens of thousands of people concludes that regular movement — from brisk walking to yoga — can ease symptoms of depression and anxiety to a degree often comparable with medication or talk therapy.
articles.image_caption: A review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found regular exercise can ease depression and anxiety as well as medication or therapy
articles.nri_angle: Mental health remains heavily stigmatised in many South Asian households, where therapy can feel taboo and antidepressants are quietly resisted — so evidence that ordinary, low-cost movement can rival those treatments offers NRI families a private, accessible first step that sidesteps both the stigma and the cost and waiting lists of formal care abroad.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Structured Lifestyle Program Slowed Brain Aging in 2,000 Older Adults — and the Recipe Is Strikingly Ordinary
articles.excerpt: In the largest lifestyle trial of its kind, the U.S. POINTER study found that a structured mix of exercise, a brain-friendly diet, mental challenge and regular health checks protected memory and thinking better than a self-guided version of the same habits.
articles.image_caption: The U.S. POINTER trial paired the MIND diet, rich in leafy greens, berries and nuts, with exercise and brain training to protect cognition
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry an elevated and earlier-onset risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and vascular disease — the very conditions that feed cognitive decline — and the trial's brain-protective diet leans on leafy greens, beans, nuts and whole grains that map closely onto a home-cooked Indian kitchen, making this one of the rare prevention strategies the diaspora can adopt without abandoning its own food.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Microplastics May Hit the Liver Hardest When the Diet Is Already Rich, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: University of Oklahoma researchers report that a common plastic doubled markers of liver injury in mice on a high-fat diet compared with the same particles on a standard diet — the clearest sign yet that microplastics and a rich diet may compound each other's harm.
articles.image_caption: Fried, fatty fast food — a new study links microplastic exposure to greater liver harm when the diet is already high in fat
articles.nri_angle: Fatty liver disease is quietly common in Indian-origin populations, who develop it at lower body weights than other groups, and diaspora kitchens lean heavily on plastic — takeaway containers, cling film, bottled water and reheated leftovers — so a finding that microplastics may bite hardest precisely when the diet is rich speaks directly to a community already at elevated metabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Painkiller in Your Medicine Cabinet May Be Quietly Taxing Your Heart and Kidneys, New Research Warns
articles.excerpt: A run of new studies — including a Danish analysis of more than six million adults — finds that everyday pain relievers such as diclofenac, ibuprofen and naproxen can raise the risk of heart attacks, strokes and kidney strain, especially in people who already have heart trouble or diabetes.
articles.image_caption: New research links common painkillers such as ibuprofen, naproxen and diclofenac to raised heart and kidney risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry an unusually high burden of early heart disease and diabetes, and over-the-counter painkillers are a fixture of NRI medicine cabinets — reached for at the first headache, body ache or fever — so a body of research showing these common drugs can quietly strain the very organs the community is most vulnerable in is a direct, practical caution for diaspora households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: It Is Not Just How Many Fruits You Eat, but Which Ones — a Study of 30,000 Adults Points to a Missing Nutrient
articles.excerpt: An international team tracking more than 30,000 adults in the US and UK found that fewer than one in five people get enough flavanols — the heart-protective compounds packed into berries, apples, broad beans and green tea — even among those who already eat their five-a-day.
articles.image_caption: Flavanol-rich foods such as berries, apples and green tea were linked to better heart health in a 30,000-adult study
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry one of the world's highest burdens of early heart disease, and many diaspora households equate 'eating healthy' with simply piling on fruit and vegetables — so a finding that the specific foods rich in flavanols (green tea, apples with the skin, berries, broad beans) matter more than raw servings offers NRIs a precise, low-cost lever for the one disease that hits their community hardest and youngest.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Common Vitamin May Be Quietly Shaping How the Brain Ages, a Study of 2,000 Older Adults Finds
articles.excerpt: Older adults with higher blood levels of vitamin C had better-preserved gray matter and stronger connections in a key memory network, Japanese researchers report — the first study to tie measured vitamin C in the blood, not just diet surveys, directly to brain structure.
articles.image_caption: Citrus fruits and leafy vegetables are key sources of vitamin C, which a Japanese study tied to better-preserved brain structure
articles.nri_angle: Vegetarian and predominantly plant-based diets are common across Indian diaspora households, and the citrus fruits, berries, tomatoes and green leafy vegetables that supply vitamin C are kitchen staples — so a finding that blood levels of this everyday nutrient track with healthier brain ageing speaks directly to NRI families thinking about how to protect memory and cognition in their parents and themselves.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Few Cups of Coffee a Day May Be Quietly Guarding Your Heart, a Study of 468,000 Adults Finds
articles.excerpt: Drinking up to three cups of coffee a day was linked to a 17 percent lower risk of dying from heart disease and a 21 percent lower stroke risk, according to a long-running analysis of nearly half a million adults — a reassuring finding for a diaspora that runs on filter coffee and chai alike.
articles.image_caption: A UK Biobank analysis of 468,629 adults linked moderate coffee intake to lower heart disease and stroke risk
articles.nri_angle: Coffee and chai are woven into daily diaspora life — South Indian filter coffee, the office cortado, the evening cup of tea — yet many Indians carry an inherited wariness that caffeine strains the heart, so robust evidence that moderate coffee is protective rather than harmful speaks directly to how NRI households think about their morning ritual.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: When You Stop Eating at Night May Matter as Much as What You Eat, a Northwestern Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Adults at higher cardiometabolic risk who stopped eating three hours before bed, dimmed the lights and extended their overnight fast by about two hours saw their sleeping blood pressure fall 3.5 percent and heart rate drop 5 percent — without changing a single calorie.
articles.image_caption: A Northwestern study found stopping food three hours before bed lowered overnight blood pressure and heart rate
articles.nri_angle: Late dinners are a cultural norm in many Indian households — 9 or 10 pm meals, often heavy, are routine — and South Asians carry outsized rates of high blood pressure and diabetes, so a finding that simply shifting the last meal earlier can improve overnight heart health offers a low-cost lever that fits diaspora life without demanding a new diet.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hormone Therapy May Quietly Be Protecting Older Women's Bones, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Postmenopausal women on hormone therapy were about 69 percent less likely to have low bone density in their hips and spine, according to research presented at the Endocrine Society's annual meeting — a reminder that menopause reshapes the skeleton long before any fracture.
articles.image_caption: Researchers found postmenopausal women on hormone therapy had far lower odds of low bone density on DXA scans
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women tend to reach lower peak bone mass and develop osteoporosis at younger ages and lower body weights than many other groups, yet hormone therapy remains stigmatised and under-discussed in many Indian families — making this fresh evidence on its skeletal benefits especially relevant for NRI women navigating menopause far from extended family support.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Carrying Extra Weight Does Not Just Raise Dementia Risk — It May Directly Cause It, a Study of 500,000 People Finds
articles.excerpt: Using a genetics-based method that mimics a randomised trial, researchers concluded that high body weight and high blood pressure are not merely warning signs but direct causes of vascular dementia — making them, in the authors' words, an “unexploited opportunity” for prevention.
articles.image_caption: A study of more than 500,000 people linked high BMI and blood pressure directly to vascular dementia risk
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry abdominal fat and develop high blood pressure and diabetes at lower body-mass thresholds than other populations, often a decade earlier — so a study identifying excess weight and hypertension as direct, modifiable causes of dementia speaks straight to a diaspora that already lives with elevated cardiometabolic risk.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Testosterone Alone Won't Fix Diabetes Risk in Older Men, a New Follow-Up Finds — the Lifestyle Still Has to Change
articles.excerpt: A long-running Australian trial found that testosterone can improve body composition, blood sugar and libido in older men with belly fat and prediabetes — but only when paired with diet and exercise, not as a shortcut around them.
articles.image_caption: A long-running trial found testosterone aids diabetes-risk reduction only alongside diet and exercise, not as a substitute
articles.nri_angle: South Asian men carry an outsized burden of type 2 diabetes and abdominal obesity, often at lower body weights than other groups — and as testosterone therapy is marketed ever more aggressively to middle-aged NRIs, this study is a timely reminder that there is no hormonal shortcut around diet and exercise.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Hormone-Disrupting Chemicals Are Turning Up in Breast Milk and Babies' Urine, a New Study Finds
articles.excerpt: Researchers who tested 336 mother-infant pairs found BPA, phthalates, parabens and pesticides in breast milk and in infants' bodies through their first six months — a reminder that everyday products carry hidden chemical passengers.
articles.image_caption: A study of 336 mother-infant pairs detected BPA, phthalates and parabens in breast milk and infant urine
articles.nri_angle: Young diaspora families juggling plastic food containers, imported cosmetics and personal-care products will want to read this carefully — the chemicals the study tracked are common in exactly the everyday items that fill NRI households, and the researchers stress this is a call to reduce exposure, not to stop breastfeeding.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Cutting Sugar Out Completely May Backfire on Your Gut, a New Study Warns
articles.excerpt: Researchers who fed mice a diet with no table sugar at all found their gut bacteria fell out of balance and inflammation rose — a caution for anyone who treats 'zero sugar' as the holy grail of healthy eating.
articles.image_caption: A 16-week mouse study found that a totally sucrose-free diet disrupted gut bacteria and raised inflammation
articles.nri_angle: Sugar has become the villain in many health-conscious NRI kitchens, where 'no sugar' is now a badge of discipline — but this research suggests that scrubbing sucrose out entirely, rather than simply eating less of it, may quietly unsettle the gut.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Drug Designed to Mend Broken Hearts May Also Heal Damaged Kidneys, Early Research Suggests
articles.excerpt: An experimental UCLA compound built to help hearts recover after a heart attack appears to repair injured kidney tissue too — a tantalising prospect for the millions of South Asians living with both heart and kidney disease.
articles.image_caption: UCLA's experimental drug AD-NP1, designed to repair heart tissue, also healed injured kidneys in mice
articles.nri_angle: South Asians carry a famously high burden of both heart disease and chronic kidney disease — conditions that often travel together with diabetes — so a single drug that might help repair both organs is exactly the kind of breakthrough that could one day matter in NRI households.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: That Long Afternoon Nap May Be Quietly Stressing a Diabetic's Liver, a New Study Warns
articles.excerpt: Researchers tracking people with type 2 diabetes found that daytime naps longer than 30 minutes were linked to a higher risk of fatty liver disease — and combined with poor night sleep, the risk more than tripled.
articles.image_caption: A study of people with type 2 diabetes linked daytime naps over 30 minutes to higher fatty-liver risk
articles.nri_angle: The afternoon nap is woven into Indian family life — the post-lunch 'aaram' is practically a cultural institution — even as type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease run rampant through the community. A study suggesting that long naps may be quietly raising liver-disease risk in diabetics speaks directly to a habit most NRI households never think twice about.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Two Hours of Lifting a Week Cut Women's Heart-Attack Risk by 44 Percent, a Harvard Study of 117,000 Women Finds
articles.excerpt: A new analysis in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology followed women for decades and found that resistance training delivered outsized protection against heart disease — a finding with particular weight for South Asian women, who face heart trouble earlier and harder.
articles.image_caption: A Harvard study of 117,000 women found two hours of resistance training a week cut heart-attack risk by 44%
articles.nri_angle: South Asian women carry an elevated, often under-recognised risk of heart disease, yet strength training remains culturally coded as a man's pursuit in many Indian families. A landmark study showing that just two hours of lifting a week slashes women's heart-attack risk speaks directly to a community where the gym is rarely seen as a place for mothers and aunties — and where the cost of that gap is measured in early heart disease.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Ozempic's Active Ingredient May Quietly Be Protecting Bones, a Study of 60,000 Diabetics Finds
articles.excerpt: Stanford researchers comparing semaglutide against other weight-loss drugs in people with type 2 diabetes found a 15 percent lower fracture risk — a reassuring twist for a community where diabetes is rampant and bones are already thinner.
articles.image_caption: A semaglutide injection pen; a study of 60,000 diabetics linked the drug to 15% fewer fractures
articles.nri_angle: Indians are among the most diabetes-prone people on earth and tend to have lower bone density than Western populations, so a finding that a wildly popular weight-loss drug many NRIs are already taking may also guard against fractures speaks directly to two health risks the diaspora carries at once.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Non-Hormone Pill for Menopause Just Passed Its First Real-World Test — on Hot Flashes and Mood Alike
articles.excerpt: In a study of 656 women, the FDA-approved drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes, night sweats, anxiety and depression within weeks — an option that matters for the many South Asian women who avoid or cannot take hormone therapy.
articles.image_caption: A study of 656 women found the non-hormone drug fezolinetant eased hot flashes and mood within weeks
articles.nri_angle: Menopause remains a taboo, under-treated subject in many Indian families, and cultural wariness about hormone therapy leaves countless diaspora women suffering in silence — so evidence that a non-hormonal pill measurably eases hot flashes, sleep loss and mood is exactly the kind of option that could reach women who would never consider hormones.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: The Smartwatch on Your Wrist May Be Quietly Doing Your Heart a Favour, a Review of 14 Trials Finds
articles.excerpt: Pooling 14 clinical trials, researchers found that heart-disease patients who used fitness apps or wearables walked nearly 1,100 more steps a day than those who did not — a small, low-cost nudge with outsized relevance for a community that develops heart disease early.
articles.image_caption: A fitness tracker; a review of 14 trials found heart patients using such tools walked about 1,100 more steps daily
articles.nri_angle: People of Indian origin suffer heart attacks up to a decade earlier than other populations and are among the most enthusiastic adopters of smartwatches and fitness rings — so the finding that a device many NRIs already wear can measurably push them to move more turns a gadget on the wrist into a genuine, low-cost cardiac-prevention tool for the diaspora.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: A Head Injury Can Raise the Risk of Brain Disease. New Research Says the Danger May Run Both Ways.
articles.excerpt: A study of more than 55,000 older veterans finds that those recently diagnosed with stroke, dementia, epilepsy or Parkinson's were far more likely to have suffered a traumatic brain injury — a finding that reframes fall prevention as brain protection for ageing parents.
articles.image_caption: An older adult walking with support; falls are the main cause of traumatic brain injury in the elderly
articles.nri_angle: Millions of NRIs are caring for ageing parents — some living abroad with them, many supporting elders back in India from a distance — and this research delivers a sharp, actionable warning: a parent newly diagnosed with dementia, stroke, epilepsy or Parkinson's is in a high-risk window for a fall-related head injury, making home fall-proofing one of the most concrete things a diaspora family can do.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Carrying Extra Weight Now Linked to 19 Cancers, Not 13 — and South Asians Show Up in the Fine Print
articles.excerpt: Pooling more than 1.5 million cancer cases across 23 countries, a sweeping new review widens the list of weight-related cancers and finds the risks differ sharply by sex and region — with striking gaps in data on South Asian populations.
articles.image_caption: A waist measurement; a review of 1.5 million cancer cases links higher BMI to 19 cancer types
articles.nri_angle: South Asians develop diabetes and heart disease at lower body weights than Western populations, yet this very review flags that South Asia is badly under-represented in long-term cancer data — meaning diaspora families are being handed risk numbers built largely on European and East Asian bodies, and should treat even a modest waistline as a cancer-prevention issue, not just a cosmetic one.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk

articles.title: Weight-Loss Drugs May Do Something Unexpected for Men: Lift Testosterone and Improve Sperm
articles.excerpt: Early data presented at a major endocrinology meeting suggests GLP-1 medicines like Ozempic may raise testosterone and improve sperm quality in men with obesity — a tentative finding in a field where male fertility is rarely discussed openly.
articles.image_caption: A GLP-1 injection pen; early data suggests the weight-loss drugs may improve testosterone and sperm quality in men
articles.nri_angle: Male infertility is one of the most stigmatised and silently borne health issues in Indian families, where the burden of childlessness is too often placed on women; framing it as a treatable, hormonally-influenced medical condition — one that weight and metabolic health can move — gives diaspora couples a less shame-laden, more clinical way to seek help.
articles.author: Diaspora Desk
